query:
ADVERSARIAL REVIEW REQUEST, with a Socratic opening. Please try to BREAK the
objective-function choice below, not to confirm it. We are about to print a
second batch of nine 3D-printed tensegrity specimens whose designs were
suggested by a Bayesian-optimization model built on this choice; we would
rather learn now that the objectives or the noise model are wrong than after
another 900 drops. Where you agree, say so briefly; spend your effort on what
is wrong, unsupported, ill-posed, or confounded.

IMPORTANT ORDERING INSTRUCTION (this is the Socratic part): Section A below
asks you to derive your own answer FROM THE NUMERIC DATA FILES ONLY (the
CSVs and the two metrics JSONs) plus the rig description in this prompt,
and to commit to it in writing, BEFORE you read our analysis markdown files
or the later sections of this prompt. Our own reasoning documents are in the
attached bundle and you will need them for sections B onward, but your
section-A answer must be recorded first and must not be revised afterwards:
if your view changes after reading our documents, record the change as an
explicit diff ("after reading, I would change X because Y"), so we can see
what the data alone supports versus what our framing talked you into.

=== CONTEXT: THE RIG AND THE CAMPAIGN ===

We drop-test small 3D-printed tensegrity unit cells ("T3 prism", ~50-100 mm
tall, 18-22 g printed, PLA struts + TPU 85A tendons) as impact attenuators.
A carriage drops 60 in onto a 1/2 in polyurethane mat. Instrumentation
(Vishay/PCB TP4): CH5, single-axis accelerometer on the bottom acrylic plate
(the INPUT, 150 G trigger); CH2/CH3/CH4, tri-axis accelerometer wax-seated in
a printed key-seat at the specimen's TOP vertex (the OUTPUT). Captures are
1.25 MHz, 100 ms records, 2 ms pre-trigger. SAE J211 phaseless Butterworth
filtering; CFC-180 is the primary band.

Round 1 of a Bayesian-optimization campaign is done: 9 designs from a scrambled
Sobol batch over 5 geometric parameters (base radius R 25-40 mm, height H
60-110 mm, twist 40-80 deg, strut diameter 6-12 mm, cable diameter 3-5.5 mm),
all projected to constant solid-CAD mass, printed once each (n = 1 article per
design), plus one off-Sobol reference design. 8 specimens tested so far, 101
drops each, first 2 drops discarded as warm-up.

Per-drop metrics available in the bundle (campaign_metrics.json has every
drop; campaign_summary.csv aka t3-prism-bo-batch-drop-results.csv has
per-specimen mean and sd; the 10 series-table CSVs are the TP4 instrument's
own independent per-event peak/duration/delta-v):

  t180        peak(CFC-180 top resultant) / peak(CFC-180 base input), per drop
  t1000       same at CFC-1000
  out_180_g   filtered output peak, G      in_180_g   filtered input peak, G
  in_dv_ms    input delta-v, m/s (full-pulse integral)
  t_second_ms time from the main impact to a second impact event, ms
  e_rebound   g * t_second / (2 * delta_v), dimensionless
  fn_hz, zeta_pct  ringdown fit of the top-vertex decay (usable on only
              5 of 8 specimens; treat as opportunistic)

Known replication scales, measured on this rig in earlier studies (documents
in the bundle): repeat drops of one article within a session give T CV
0.2-0.5 percent; re-mounting the same article across sessions moves T up to
~2 percent (measured twice in this campaign: 0.13 and 0.58 percent); printing
the same geometry again moves T by ~2 percent (five nominally identical
prints, print-defect study attached). The largest design-to-design spread in
this campaign is 16.8 percent in t180 and 2.5x in e_rebound.

One tested specimen (amdjwm, the second-best t180 at 0.980) cannot be mapped
to any design and its parameters are unknown; it is excluded from the BO
training set. Its t_second/e_rebound values are also flagged unreliable in
this session.

=== A. SOCRATIC OPENING: DERIVE, DO NOT REVIEW (numeric files + this context
       only; do this before reading our markdown documents) ===

The engineering goal: find the design that best protects a payload from a
single impact of this severity. The BO loop prints 9 new designs per round.

 A1. From the per-drop data, which measured quantity or quantities would YOU
     optimize? One objective or several? For each candidate in the list
     above (and any derived quantity you would construct from them), say
     whether it is (a) a valid objective, (b) a constraint or diagnostic,
     or (c) unusable, and why. Consider at least: ratio vs absolute output
     peak given the input varies (in_180_g spans 202-236 G across specimens);
     what e_rebound = g*t_second/(2*dv) physically is (note: is it an energy
     ratio, a velocity ratio, or something else? does its label matter?);
     and whether t180 and e_rebound are independent enough pieces of physics
     to justify a Pareto treatment, or two projections of one underlying
     compliance axis.
 A2. From the 8 specimens' data, is a MULTI-objective (Pareto) formulation
     warranted, or does one objective dominate/subsume the other? Quantify:
     what is the correlation structure between the candidate objectives
     across specimens and how sensitive is it to any single specimen?
 A3. What noise magnitude would you attach to each per-design observation
     handed to a Gaussian-process-based optimizer, given the three
     replication scales above and n = 1 article per design? Give a number
     or a formula, and justify the replication unit you chose.
 A4. Record your committed answers to A1-A3 in a clearly-marked block.

=== WHAT WE ACTUALLY DID (read only after committing section A) ===

Our BO script (bundle: t3_prism_bo_campaign.py) runs Ax/BoTorch SAASBO with
qNEHVI, two objectives, both MINIMIZED: t180 and e_rebound. Noise per design
is passed as the per-drop SEM: sd of the ~99 valid drops divided by sqrt(99),
i.e. ~0.0004 on t180 (~0.04 percent of the value) and ~1e-4 on e_rebound. The
~2 percent print-to-print floor is acknowledged in a comment and NOT modeled.
7 completed observations were attached (6 mapped Sobol designs + the
reference design), amdjwm was skipped, and the 3 printed-but-untested designs
were attached as pending so the acquisition avoids them. The resulting round-2
suggestions put 8 of 9 designs at the 12 mm strut-diameter bound and 7 of 9 at
the 60 mm height bound.

The claim under review, verbatim from our hand-off comment:

  "Objectives: minimize t180 and minimize e_rebound, per the BO hand-off
  section of the campaign analysis doc and the #97 energy-absorption framing.
  The multi-objective assumption holds in the data: they genuinely trade off
  (best attenuator 6lhxfy hops hardest at e_rebound 0.050), so the Pareto
  front is informative. Noise is passed as per-drop SEM; the ~2 percent
  print-to-print floor (n = 1 article per design) is noted but not modeled."

=== B. ATTACK e_rebound AS AN OBJECTIVE ===

 B1. Dimensional and physical audit of e_rebound = g*t_second/(2*delta_v).
     Derive what this quantity actually is for a ballistic hop. Is calling
     it "rebound ENERGY ratio" correct? If it is really a velocity ratio,
     does the mislabeling change the optimizer's behavior (monotone
     transforms preserve a Pareto set), the noise model (SEM of v vs v^2),
     or only the physical interpretation and thresholds?
 B2. WHAT is hopping, and whose energy is it? t_second is the delay to a
     second impact event. Establish from the data (series tables, per-drop
     records) whether the second event is the specimen leaving the plate and
     landing again, the carriage bouncing on the mat, or something else,
     and whether that distinction survives across specimens. If the hop is
     substantially the carriage/mat restitution rather than the specimen's,
     minimizing it optimizes the fixture, not the design.
 B3. Direction-of-goodness. For a payload-protection objective, argue both
     sides: (i) rebound energy returned to the payload is injury/damage
     energy, minimize it; (ii) a specimen that stores impact energy
     elastically and returns it as a hop has diverted it from the
     transmitted-peak path, which is exactly what the best attenuator did,
     so penalizing the hop double-counts against the mechanism that works.
     Which is right FOR THIS RIG, where the "payload" surrogate is the
     top-vertex accelerometer and the specimen itself hops?
 B4. amdjwm's e_rebound is flagged unreliable because its t_second detection
     was unstable (sd 15.7 ms vs <1 ms for others). How fragile is the
     t_second detector generally, and does e_rebound remain a usable
     objective for designs whose second impact is soft or split?

=== C. ATTACK THE TRADE-OFF / PARETO CLAIM ===

 C1. With 8 specimens (7 in the training set), quantify the association
     between t180 and e_rebound and its dependence on single points. Redo it
     without 6lhxfy, without bag26v, and rank-based. Does "they genuinely
     trade off" survive?
 C2. Even if anti-correlated across THESE 8 designs, is that a trade-off in
     the decision-relevant sense (a Pareto FRONT of mutually non-dominated
     optima), or a 1-D physical coupling (softer tendon path -> lower
     transmitted peak AND bigger hop) along which one direction is simply
     better? What would each hypothesis predict for the round-2 batch, and
     what in the existing data discriminates them?
 C3. If the trade-off is not supported: what does the qNEHVI acquisition do
     when handed two near-deterministic, strongly-coupled objectives, and
     does that explain the suggested batch collapsing onto the strut/height
     bounds (8 of 9 at strut 12 mm, 7 of 9 at H 60 mm)?

=== D. ATTACK THE NOISE MODEL. This is our biggest worry. ===

 D1. The observation handed to the GP for a design is one printed article's
     101-drop mean with SEM ~0.04 percent, but the design-level replication
     floor (print-to-print) is ~2 percent, i.e. the stated noise understates
     the decision-relevant noise by roughly 50x. Work through what this does
     to a SAASBO fit on 7 points in 5-D and to qNEHVI: interpolation of
     print-lottery noise as signal, overconfident Pareto membership,
     boundary-seeking suggestions? Connect to the actual round-2 batch.
 D2. Is the ~2 percent floor itself well-founded? Audit the attached
     print-defect study (5 nominally identical prints): is 2 percent a sd,
     a spread, a CV; on which metric; does it transfer to e_rebound (what is
     the print-to-print floor for e_rebound, and can the bundle's two
     double-session specimens bound the re-mount contribution)?
 D3. Give the correct noise treatment for round 2 concretely: e.g. pass
     SEM combined in quadrature with a design-level floor per objective
     (state the numbers you would use), or let the GP infer noise instead
     of fixing it, or model article and session as hierarchy. Which is
     defensible in the Ax Service API with fewer than 10 points, and what
     do you predict changes in the suggestions when the fix is applied?
 D4. n = 1 article per design and 101 drops per article: given the three
     replication scales, was that the right allocation, and what allocation
     (articles x drops) should round 2 use for the same total effort?

=== E. ATTACK t180 ITSELF, IN LIGHT OF NEW EVIDENCE ===

An earlier adversarial review on this rig (of a mat-arrangement sweep, 20 ms
truncated records, different mat states) concluded near-unity T was likely a
rigid-body pulse-transmission ratio and questioned peak-ratio T as a BO
objective. Since then: records are 100 ms with 2 ms pre-trigger and a
validated tail re-baseline, and this campaign measured t180 0.893-1.062 with
within-specimen CV 0.2-0.5 percent and clean cross-session transfer (0.13 and
0.58 percent), while t1000 does NOT transfer across sessions.

 E1. Does the 16.8 percent design spread with sub-percent repeatability
     settle the earlier objection that T does not see the structure, or can
     a mount/seating artifact still produce a specimen-STABLE, design-
     correlated t180? What in the bundle discriminates?
 E2. Peak-ratio vs alternatives now practically available in these 100 ms
     records (SRS ratio at the payload band, band-limited transmissibility,
     transmitted impulse ratio, output peak at measured input): would any
     change the RANKING of these 8 specimens? If the ranking is invariant,
     say so; that is a defense of t180 we would like tested, not assumed.

=== F. WHAT IS MISSING ===

 F1. Should anything measured but unused enter the formulation: absolute
     out_180_g as the objective with in_180_g as context/covariate; t1000 as
     a constraint (broadband amplifiers autv5r/nvxsrv hit 1.23-1.24); mass
     or printed-mass-normalized metrics, given constant solid mass produced
     an 18.5-22 g printed spread; fn/zeta where usable?
 F2. Excluding amdjwm (2nd-best t180) from training because its parameters
     are unknown: any way to use it (e.g. as an outcome-only observation,
     or measuring its geometry post hoc), and how much information is lost?

=== G. VERDICT ===

State, in order: (1) your section-A committed answer and whether reading our
documents changed it; (2) which of the three legs of the quoted claim survive
(objective pair; genuine trade-off/Pareto informativeness; per-drop-SEM noise
model); (3) the corrected formulation you would run for round 2, concretely
(objectives with directions, constraints, noise numbers, any re-allocation of
articles vs drops); (4) whether the committed round-2 suggestions should be
printed as-is, re-generated after fixes, or gated on a cheap intermediate
experiment, and if the latter, which experiment. Anchor in standard practice
where relevant (SAE J211 for filtering, shock-isolation practice for
transmissibility and SRS, coefficient-of-restitution practice for rebound
measurement, and the BO literature on noise handling: SAASBO, qNEHVI,
heteroskedastic/hierarchical noise).

Attached bundle: campaign_summary CSV (= t3-prism-bo-batch-drop-results.csv),
campaign_metrics.json (per-drop rows, 8 specimens), partial_sessions_
metrics.json (the two interrupted-session re-runs), 10 TP4 series-table CSVs
(instrument-independent per-event peaks/durations/delta-v), params.json and
dataset README, our campaign analysis doc and analysis script, the print-
defect study, the PR #97 energy-absorption review, the BO script, its round-2
suggestions CSV, the Sobol design table, and the print key.

Output a single self-contained markdown report we can commit under
edison-trajectories/bo-objectives/. Lead with the conclusions that CHANGE
what we print next.

info.name: run_cell
info.description:
Run code in a notebook cell and return the execution output.

This method allows running code in a new cell (append) or re-running
an existing cell with updated code.

Usage Examples:
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Creating example code") # Run code in new cell
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Modifying example code",
            idx=0) # Run code in existing cell at index 0

Error Recovery:
    When a cell fails with an error, you MUST fix it by calling run_cell
    with the corrected code and the SAME idx as the failed cell:

    run_cell("corrected_code", idx=3)  # Fix error in Cell #3

    The cell number is shown in the output prefix (e.g., "[Cell #3]").
    Do NOT create a new cell to fix an error - always edit the failed cell.

display_text.description:
A short, ~100 character gerund phrase describing
the code intent for the end user.
display_text.title: Display Text

idx.description:
Cell index to run. If None or >= len(cells), appends a new cell.
If provided, updates and re-runs the existing cell at that index.
Use this to fix errors in existing cells.
idx.title: Idx

info.name: reset_kernel
info.description:
Reset the kernel to a clean state.

This clears all variables and execution state while preserving notebook history.

_unused.description:
Unused. Present so the tool schema has a property — OpenAI's
Responses API rejects zero-arg tools with "object schema missing
properties".
_unused.title: Unused

info.name: submit_answer
info.description: Submit your response to the research question.

answer.description: Your final response to the research question
answer.title: Answer

info.name: read
info.description:
Read file contents with line numbers.

Reads text files, source code, config files, images, PDFs, PowerPoint,
Word documents, and Jupyter notebooks. For binary data files (Excel,
databases, Parquet, etc.), use Python code instead.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines/pages to read
limit.title: Limit

offset.description:
Start line (0-based) for text, or start page/slide (1-based) for PDFs/PowerPoint/
Word documents
offset.title: Offset

info.name: explore
info.description:
Search the workspace or memory for information.

Spawns a lightweight sub-agent that can read files, grep, jq, and
run shell pipelines to find information in the workspace. Use this
instead of reading large files or exploring directories directly —
the sub-agent manages its own context so your context is not consumed.

What the sub-agent CAN do: list directories, read text and multimedia
files (PDFs, powerpoints, images), grep/jq/filter file contents, and
retrieve prior conversation history that has scrolled out of your context.

What the sub-agent CANNOT do: execute Python or R, modify the filesystem,
invoke external binaries (unzip, CLI tools, package installs), or perform
numerical computation or statistical analysis — those are your job with
`run_cell`.

Note: the sub-agent is a weaker model than you, so focus on using it for
information retrieval, but not complex analysis, reasoning, or decision-making.
You should be responsible for those activities, based on information the
sub-agent retrieves at your direction. If it reports that a result is not
stored on disk, that describes the workspace — run the computation yourself
with `run_cell` rather than treating it as a stop condition.

Common uses:
- Retrieve information from conversation memory after compaction or reset.
- Search large log or data files for specific entries
- Summarize contents of files you haven't read yet
- Retrieve outputs or conversation history from a completed sub-agent
  task.

query.description:
What to find or summarize, e.g. "What datasets have I
downloaded so far?" or "Have I seen error X before, and how did I solve it?".
query.title: Query

info.name: view_docs
info.description:
Look up e14c API documentation for one or more modules, classes, or functions.

Browse top-down: start with "e14c" to see available modules, then
drill into specific modules. Use verbose=False to navigate the tree;
only use verbose=True on specific targets you've already identified.
Do not call view_docs speculatively at the start of a task — call it
just-in-time as you need specific APIs. Batch related lookups into a
single call, e.g. ``view_docs(["e14c.filesystem", "e14c.shell"])``.

verbose.description: If False, compact listing. If True, full signatures and docstrings.
verbose.title: Verbose

info.name: load_skill
info.description:
Load a skill guide by name.

Returns the full content of the skill's SKILL.md file, which
contains instructions, code examples, and best practices for
using the skill.

skill_name.description: Name of the skill to load (e.g. "edison").
skill_name.title: Skill Name

messages.content:
You are a rigorous data analysis agent with deep expertise in statistics, data science, and quantitative methods. Your primary directive is to provide accurate, evidence-based analysis in Jupyter notebooks while maintaining the highest standards of scientific integrity.

## Core Principles

**Do not fabricate data for any reason**

You must never invent, simulate, or fabricate data under any circumstances. All analyses, visualizations, and interpretations must be directly derivable from the provided dataset or data correctly pulled in from external sources (eg. gene annotations, external databases). If you cannot access required data you must report this limitation and end the analysis. You must not subsample data without an analytical or technical purpose. If the data must be subsampled due to memory limitations or other technical constraints, this must be justified and reported.

**All analyses must demonstrate statistical rigor and methodological excellence**

Every analytical procedure must be statistically sound and suitable for the specific data type and research question being addressed. You should always consider and mention underlying statistical assumptions (normality, independence, homoscedasticity, etc.). You must check assumptions before applying statistical tests and report when assumptions are violated. You should use correct statistical terminology, notation, and precision in reporting. You must report relevant metrics: p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, test statistics, degrees of freedom. You should apply appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons when necessary. You must distinguish between correlation and causation, avoiding causal claims from observational data.

**Report the limitations of the data and your analysis**

If a request is beyond your capabilities or the scope of provided data, you must state this clearly and concisely. You should never attempt to answer questions requiring domain knowledge you do not possess or cannot acquire through use of tools such as external data sources or web search. You must acknowledge limitations of methods, sample sizes, and data quality. You should communicate uncertainty and confidence levels explicitly.

**Never fabricate solutions when you cannot complete a task**

If you cannot do something, you must never fabricate a solution. You should clearly state what you cannot do and why, rather than providing false or misleading information.

**Be concise and focused in your analysis**

You should address the research question directly and efficiently. You must avoid extraneous information that doesn't contribute to answering the question. You should present findings with appropriate statistical precision (don't over-report decimal places). You must provide concrete, quantitative evidence with specific values that support or refute hypotheses.

You are operating in a production execution environment with internet access and tools for data analysis, API calls, and data retrieval.

You do not have access to GPUs or specialized hardware, and you are limited to 3600 seconds of runtime.

Execution resource limits:
- cpu limit: 10
- memory limit: 32Gi
- /workspace directory limit: 50Gi
- /tmp directory limit: 15Gi
Plan execution around these limits. For large file operations, estimate peak disk usage first, including input, output, and temporary files. For memory-heavy work, estimate peak memory usage and use streaming or chunking when needed. If a plan may exceed a limit, use a smaller plan. If you exceed the memory limit or a listed directory limit, execution will be stopped and work will be lost.

## Error Response Protocol

When you cannot fulfill a request:
You must state clearly: "I cannot [specific request] because [specific limitation]"
You should explain: Brief explanation of the constraint or missing requirement
You must end analysis: Do not attempt workarounds that compromise data integrity
You should specify needs: If applicable, state what would be required to address the request properly

## Structured Analysis Protocol

Step 1: Define Analysis Plan

Outline specific data filtering, processing, and analysis steps
State the statistical methods and tests you will use
Identify potential limitations or assumptions
Example format: "1. Filter dataset for [criteria]. 2. Apply [transformation]. 3. Execute [statistical test]. 4. Interpret results against [threshold/criterion]."

Step 2: Execute the analysis plan

Execute your plan systematically, one step at a time
Follow closely the jupyter notebook implementation standards and error response protocol

Step 3: Present Quantitative Evidence

**Important: Use the submit_answer tool to respond to the research question. YOUR TASK IS NOT COMPLETE UNTIL AN ANSWER IS SUBMITTED**
Present findings with concrete, quantitative evidence
Provide specific values that define relationships or rules
Include relevant statistical metrics (correlation coefficients, p-values, effect sizes, fold changes)
Ensure evidence directly supports or refutes the research question



IMPORTANT: The core principles must be adhered to at all times. When in doubt, rather than proceeding with questionable analysis, make note of your uncertainty both in the notebook and in the answer. Scientific integrity requires absolute honesty about what can and cannot be determined from available data. It is always better to provide a limited but accurate analysis than to compromise data fidelity or statistical rigor.

# How You Work

You are Kosmos and were created by Edison Scientific. You make discoveries, mostly alone. Novel, actionable, interesting — or you haven't done your job.

## How to Think

Match effort to the ask. Simple user queries get quick, direct answers — no over-planning, no cosmetic polish, no deliberating over themes or formatting. If the user asks a question you can answer now, answer it in the most direct way possible. Overthinking simple requests wastes the user's time and your steps.

Test with data first: Edison analysis agents and your own code can check hypotheses against real datasets right now.
An Edison literature review that doesn't lead to a test is procrastination.

Contain excitement. The ideation-execution gap: ideas that sound novel fall apart in practice. For every idea — what goes wrong? What's the cheapest test? Is it novel?

## Fighting Mode Collapse

RLHF makes your output clean, hedged, pleasant. This poisons your thinking because your notes become your future thoughts.

Write messy. Half-formed ideas stay half-formed. "This feels connected to X but I can't see how" > a tidy bullet point.

Seek new information. Social media. The date. Sideways citations. People who are wrong in interesting ways.

## How to Write

Write like a researcher in a hurry. Plain, specific language: no em dash, no "delve," "moreover," or "embark." Avoid useless modifiers like "vigorously inducing."

Avoid unnecessary jargon. Do not invent new, complex, or metaphorical terms for phenomena (e.g., "Gene-Level Sentinel") when a plain description is sufficient. Spell out acronyms on first use; do not chain unexpanded acronyms with slashes (e.g., "FAERS/IP"). When you reference a private name from your own notes (e.g., project codenames), expand it in plain English the first time it appears in a turn.

No dramatic language ("marking a pivotal moment," "a significant shift," "part of a broader movement"). If something is important, show it through concrete detail.

No sales writing, no hedging with false balance. If nuance is needed, make it specific. Vary sentence length. Some sentences are short. No tidy intro-body-conclusion arcs, no "In summary" or "Overall." No "it's not X, it's Y" constructions.

## Citing Sources

Always cite sources for claims, either to a primary source or specific dataset/analysis. If trying to cite a primary source, use services like Crossref or OpenAlex to fetch bibliographic details instead of guessing.

## Vibe

Direct and helpful, never overly verbose or sycophantic. Be objective and scientific. The research speaks or it doesn't. Some humor, but polite and respectful.

# Output Format

On markdown formatting:

- Follow MARKDOWN_RENDERING.md for formatting (especially tildes) in your answer text.

On chemical formatting:

- When the answer contains a single SMILES that should display as a 2D molecule, wrap it in <smiles>...</smiles>. For multiple molecules, follow the chemistry-specific visualization rules from DATA_ANALYSIS_CHEMISTRY.md.
- Use your judgement on rendering small SMILES that are less than 4 heavy atoms. If it will be better visually, use backticks to render inline instead of <smiles>...</smiles>.

Once you have completed your analysis, submit your answer using the submit_answer tool.
Your answer must satisfy the following requirements including an answer and a decision list:

[Your complete answer]

[A bulleted list of discretionary analytical decisions made during the analysis]

**Discretionary decisions** are choices where:

- Multiple scientifically valid approaches exist
- Different researchers might reasonably choose different options
- The choice does not invalidate the analysis but may affect exact numerical results
- The decision reflects methodological judgment rather than correction of an error

Examples include:

- Statistical test selection when assumptions are borderline (e.g., "Used Mann-Whitney U test rather than t-test due to slight deviation from normality")
- Multiple testing correction method (e.g., "Applied FDR correction rather than Bonferroni")
- Significance thresholds (e.g., "Set alpha = 0.05")
- Quality control cutoffs (e.g., "Filtered genes with <10 reads across all samples")
- Normalization approach (e.g., "Applied log2 transformation before analysis")
- Database/reference version (e.g., "Used ENSEMBL v110 for gene annotations")
- Parameter values for algorithms (e.g., "Set k=5 for k-means clustering based on elbow method")
- Binning or grouping strategies for continuous variables
- Choice between multiple valid visualization scales (linear vs. log)

DO NOT include:

- Standard analytical steps that have no alternatives
- Corrections of errors or bugs
- Choices that are dictated by the data structure itself
- Software version numbers (unless the choice between versions was discretionary)

## R Code Execution (if needed)

If the task requires R code, use the `%%Rscript` cell magic. This environment uses a Python kernel, so R code must be run via this magic:

```
%%Rscript
library(tidyverse)
df <- read_csv("data.csv")
summary(df)
```

The entire cell content after `%%Rscript` is executed as R code via Rscript subprocess.

**Python↔R Data Exchange:** If you need to pass data between Python and R, use Parquet files:

- Python: `df.to_parquet("data.parquet")`
- R: `df <- arrow::read_parquet("data.parquet")`

**Displaying R Plots:** R plots are not automatically captured. To display plots:

1. Save the plot to a file in R:

   ```r
   %%Rscript
   library(ggplot2)
   p <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
   ggsave("plot.png", p, width=8, height=6, dpi=150)
   ```

2. Display the saved image in a Python cell:

   ```python
   from IPython.display import Image, display

   display(Image("plot.png"))
   ```

**R Code Style (when using R):**

- Suppress startup messages: `suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))`
- Use explicit namespaces: `dplyr::select()` instead of `select()`
- Use ggplot2 for plots

## Workspace structure

## Sub-agent functionality

### Literature

The `literature` sub-agent can perform deep searches over scientific literature, patents, and clinical trials.
It has specialized tooling (that you do not have access to) to retrieve and process many full-text documents.
In addition to an answer to your query, it will provide BibTeX-formatted citations for all source documents it relied on.
Note that the `literature` sub-agent does **not** have access to general web search.
That means it cannot access things like data repositories, blog posts, social media, company websites, and so on.
If your query requires access to such sources, consider using `e14c.web` (call `view_docs` to read more) as an alternative or complementary solution.

### Analysis

The `analysis` sub-agent can perform heavier computational tasks than you can.
It has access to a Python interpreter much like you do, but is given more CPUs and RAM.
Therefore, delegate any serious computational or data analysis tasks to it via `submit_task(agent_type="analysis")` (note that `"analysis"` is the default `agent_type`).
Also consider that once a script or library is written, the `analysis` agent can be called multiple times in parallel to execute the code with different parameterizations (e.g. a hyperparameter sweep).



### Molecules

The `molecules` sub-agent specializes in chemistry workflows and includes deeper chemistry-specific guidance and tooling. Delegate to `molecules` for any workflows that imply chemistry and cheminformatics. When the query involves chemical structures, reactions, metabolite identification, or similar tasks, look to the `molecules` sub-agent first before deciding to use other sub-agents.

### Data retrieval

The `data-retrieval` sub-agent is a specialized system for retrieving data from specific sources.
It has deeper support for a range of biological databases spanning expression, variants, structures, proteomics, pharmacology, and general data deposits — e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA, PDB, ClinVar, PRIDE, KEGG, Zenodo, among others — and can also search sources beyond that set.
Use this agent when you know either:

1. a specific data source / dataset ID (e.g. GEO accession number)
2. or have narrowed things down to a small subset of data sources and need to perform a search against them (e.g. "find me RNA-seq datasets pertaining to ...")

### Artifact generation

The `artifact-generation` sub-agent produces file deliverables across formats — reports and papers (LaTeX/markdown); slide decks (`.pptx`); Word documents (`.docx`), spreadsheets (`.xlsx`); and infographics, schematics, and diagrams. It has format-specific skills auto-loaded (`scientific-writing`, `pptx`, `docx`, `xlsx`) and uses `e14c.image_generation.generate_image` for label-heavy conceptual figures and `e14c.image_generation.generate_infographic` for non-text-heavy infographic figures. Use it whenever the deliverable is a file artifact the user will open in a specific application, or whenever you need a paper-quality non-data figure. Include the target format, allowed source task IDs/files/data entries, and any structural requirements in your dispatch query so the sub-agent routes correctly. It can delegate to `literature` for citation verification. Do not use `analysis` for artifact authoring — that agent's persona over-compresses and has no format-specific guidance.

## Dataset search and retrieval

For the specific task of dataset search and retrieval, there are multiple complementary strategies.
Decide which of the following (possibly multiple) are relevant for each search/retrieval task and apply accordingly.

- `e14c.web`: Directly search the web for broad sweeps when a relevant dataset could live across multiple sources (GitHub, Hugging Face, GEO, lab pages). Relatively fast, but may not be as deep as a literature sub-agent. Note that `e14c.web` is not a sub-agent, but rather a set of search functions you can call yourself.
- `submit_task(agent_type="literature")`: Searches scientific literature only (papers, patents, clinical trials) for publications that reference or introduce datasets. Surfaces dataset names and citations, not the data itself. Can be useful to find relevant datasets before retrieval by another method, but is slower than web search. The literature agent does not have access to general web search.
- `submit_task(agent_type="data-retrieval")`: Targeted pull from a specific source (e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA) once you already know which source and roughly what you need from it (i.e. a specific dataset ID or targeted search query).

per-specimen mean and sd; the 10 series-table CSVs are the TP4 instrument's
own independent per-event peak/duration/delta-v):

  t180        peak(CFC-180 top resultant) / peak(CFC-180 base input), per drop
  t1000       same at CFC-1000
  out_180_g   filtered output peak, G      in_180_g   filtered input peak, G
  in_dv_ms    input delta-v, m/s (full-pulse integral)
  t_second_ms time from the main impact to a second impact event, ms
  e_rebound   g * t_second / (2 * delta_v), dimensionless
  fn_hz, zeta_pct  ringdown fit of the top-vertex decay (usable on only
              5 of 8 specimens; treat as opportunistic)

Known replication scales, measured on this rig in earlier studies (documents
in the bundle): repeat drops of one article within a session give T CV
0.2-0.5 percent; re-mounting the same article across sessions moves T up to
~2 percent (measured twice in this campaign: 0.13 and 0.58 percent); printing
the same geometry again moves T by ~2 percent (five nominally identical
prints, print-defect study attached). The largest design-to-design spread in
this campaign is 16.8 percent in t180 and 2.5x in e_rebound.

One tested specimen (amdjwm, the second-best t180 at 0.980) cannot be mapped
to any design and its parameters are unknown; it is excluded from the BO
training set. Its t_second/e_rebound values are also flagged unreliable in
this session.

=== A. SOCRATIC OPENING: DERIVE, DO NOT REVIEW (numeric files + this context
       only; do this before reading our markdown documents) ===

The engineering goal: find the design that best protects a payload from a
single impact of this severity. The BO loop prints 9 new designs per round.

 A1. From the per-drop data, which measured quantity or quantities would YOU
     optimize? One objective or several? For each candidate in the list
     above (and any derived quantity you would construct from them), say
     whether it is (a) a valid objective, (b) a constraint or diagnostic,
     or (c) unusable, and why. Consider at least: ratio vs absolute output
     peak given the input varies (in_180_g spans 202-236 G across specimens);
     what e_rebound = g*t_second/(2*dv) physically is (note: is it an energy
     ratio, a velocity ratio, or something else? does its label matter?);
     and whether t180 and e_rebound are independent enough pieces of physics
     to justify a Pareto treatment, or two projections of one underlying
     compliance axis.
 A2. From the 8 specimens' data, is a MULTI-objective (Pareto) formulation
     warranted, or does one objective dominate/subsume the other? Quantify:
     what is the correlation structure between the candidate objectives
     across specimens and how sensitive is it to any single specimen?
 A3. What noise magnitude would you attach to each per-design observation
     handed to a Gaussian-process-based optimizer, given the three
     replication scales above and n = 1 article per design? Give a number
     or a formula, and justify the replication unit you chose.
 A4. Record your committed answers to A1-A3 in a clearly-marked block.

=== WHAT WE ACTUALLY DID (read only after committing section A) ===

Our BO script (bundle: t3_prism_bo_campaign.py) runs Ax/BoTorch SAASBO with
qNEHVI, two objectives, both MINIMIZED: t180 and e_rebound. Noise per design
is passed as the per-drop SEM: sd of the ~99 valid drops divided by sqrt(99),
i.e. ~0.0004 on t180 (~0.04 percent of the value) and ~1e-4 on e_rebound. The
~2 percent print-to-print floor is acknowledged in a comment and NOT modeled.
7 completed observations were attached (6 mapped Sobol designs + the
reference design), amdjwm was skipped, and the 3 printed-but-untested designs
were attached as pending so the acquisition avoids them. The resulting round-2
suggestions put 8 of 9 designs at the 12 mm strut-diameter bound and 7 of 9 at
the 60 mm height bound.

The claim under review, verbatim from our hand-off comment:

  "Objectives: minimize t180 and minimize e_rebound, per the BO hand-off
  section of the campaign analysis doc and the #97 energy-absorption framing.
  The multi-objective assumption holds in the data: they genuinely trade off
  (best attenuator 6lhxfy hops hardest at e_rebound 0.050), so the Pareto
  front is informative. Noise is passed as per-drop SEM; the ~2 percent
  print-to-print floor (n = 1 article per design) is noted but not modeled."

=== B. ATTACK e_rebound AS AN OBJECTIVE ===

 B1. Dimensional and physical audit of e_rebound = g*t_second/(2*delta_v).
     Derive what this quantity actually is for a ballistic hop. Is calling
     it "rebound ENERGY ratio" correct? If it is really a velocity ratio,
     does the mislabeling change the optimizer's behavior (monotone
     transforms preserve a Pareto set), the noise model (SEM of v vs v^2),
     or only the physical interpretation and thresholds?
 B2. WHAT is hopping, and whose energy is it? t_second is the delay to a
     second impact event. Establish from the data (series tables, per-drop
     records) whether the second event is the specimen leaving the plate and
     landing again, the carriage bouncing on the mat, or something else,
     and whether that distinction survives across specimens. If the hop is
     substantially the carriage/mat restitution rather than the specimen's,
     minimizing it optimizes the fixture, not the design.
 B3. Direction-of-goodness. For a payload-protection objective, argue both
     sides: (i) rebound energy returned to the payload is injury/damage
     energy, minimize it; (ii) a specimen that stores impact energy
     elastically and returns it as a hop has diverted it from the
     transmitted-peak path, which is exactly what the best attenuator did,
     so penalizing the hop double-counts against the mechanism that works.
     Which is right FOR THIS RIG, where the "payload" surrogate is the
     top-vertex accelerometer and the specimen itself hops?
 B4. amdjwm's e_rebound is flagged unreliable because its t_second detection
     was unstable (sd 15.7 ms vs <1 ms for others). How fragile is the
     t_second detector generally, and does e_rebound remain a usable
     objective for designs whose second impact is soft or split?

=== C. ATTACK THE TRADE-OFF / PARETO CLAIM ===

 C1. With 8 specimens (7 in the training set), quantify the association
     between t180 and e_rebound and its dependence on single points. Redo it
     without 6lhxfy, without bag26v, and rank-based. Does "they genuinely
     trade off" survive?
 C2. Even if anti-correlated across THESE 8 designs, is that a trade-off in
     the decision-relevant sense (a Pareto FRONT of mutually non-dominated
     optima), or a 1-D physical coupling (softer tendon path -> lower
     transmitted peak AND bigger hop) along which one direction is simply
     better? What would each hypothesis predict for the round-2 batch, and
     what in the existing data discriminates them?
 C3. If the trade-off is not supported: what does the qNEHVI acquisition do
     when handed two near-deterministic, strongly-coupled objectives, and
     does that explain the suggested batch collapsing onto the strut/height
     bounds (8 of 9 at strut 12 mm, 7 of 9 at H 60 mm)?

=== D. ATTACK THE NOISE MODEL. This is our biggest worry. ===

 D1. The observation handed to the GP for a design is one printed article's
     101-drop mean with SEM ~0.04 percent, but the design-level replication
     floor (print-to-print) is ~2 percent, i.e. the stated noise understates
     the decision-relevant noise by roughly 50x. Work through what this does
     to a SAASBO fit on 7 points in 5-D and to qNEHVI: interpolation of
     print-lottery noise as signal, overconfident Pareto membership,
     boundary-seeking suggestions? Connect to the actual round-2 batch.
 D2. Is the ~2 percent floor itself well-founded? Audit the attached
     print-defect study (5 nominally identical prints): is 2 percent a sd,
     a spread, a CV; on which metric; does it transfer to e_rebound (what is
     the print-to-print floor for e_rebound, and can the bundle's two
     double-session specimens bound the re-mount contribution)?
 D3. Give the correct noise treatment for round 2 concretely: e.g. pass
     SEM combined in quadrature with a design-level floor per objective
     (state the numbers you would use), or let the GP infer noise instead
     of fixing it, or model article and session as hierarchy. Which is
     defensible in the Ax Service API with fewer than 10 points, and what
     do you predict changes in the suggestions when the fix is applied?
 D4. n = 1 article per design and 101 drops per article: given the three
     replication scales, was that the right allocation, and what allocation
     (articles x drops) should round 2 use for the same total effort?

=== E. ATTACK t180 ITSELF, IN LIGHT OF NEW EVIDENCE ===

An earlier adversarial review on this rig (of a mat-arrangement sweep, 20 ms
truncated records, different mat states) concluded near-unity T was likely a
rigid-body pulse-transmission ratio and questioned peak-ratio T as a BO
objective. Since then: records are 100 ms with 2 ms pre-trigger and a
validated tail re-baseline, and this campaign measured t180 0.893-1.062 with
within-specimen CV 0.2-0.5 percent and clean cross-session transfer (0.13 and
0.58 percent), while t1000 does NOT transfer across sessions.

 E1. Does the 16.8 percent design spread with sub-percent repeatability
     settle the earlier objection that T does not see the structure, or can
     a mount/seating artifact still produce a specimen-STABLE, design-
     correlated t180? What in the bundle discriminates?
 E2. Peak-ratio vs alternatives now practically available in these 100 ms
     records (SRS ratio at the payload band, band-limited transmissibility,
     transmitted impulse ratio, output peak at measured input): would any
     change the RANKING of these 8 specimens? If the ranking is invariant,
     say so; that is a defense of t180 we would like tested, not assumed.

=== F. WHAT IS MISSING ===

 F1. Should anything measured but unused enter the formulation: absolute
     out_180_g as the objective with in_180_g as context/covariate; t1000 as
     a constraint (broadband amplifiers autv5r/nvxsrv hit 1.23-1.24); mass
     or printed-mass-normalized metrics, given constant solid mass produced
     an 18.5-22 g printed spread; fn/zeta where usable?
 F2. Excluding amdjwm (2nd-best t180) from training because its parameters
     are unknown: any way to use it (e.g. as an outcome-only observation,
     or measuring its geometry post hoc), and how much information is lost?

=== G. VERDICT ===

State, in order: (1) your section-A committed answer and whether reading our
documents changed it; (2) which of the three legs of the quoted claim survive
(objective pair; genuine trade-off/Pareto informativeness; per-drop-SEM noise
model); (3) the corrected formulation you would run for round 2, concretely
(objectives with directions, constraints, noise numbers, any re-allocation of
articles vs drops); (4) whether the committed round-2 suggestions should be
printed as-is, re-generated after fixes, or gated on a cheap intermediate
experiment, and if the latter, which experiment. Anchor in standard practice
where relevant (SAE J211 for filtering, shock-isolation practice for
transmissibility and SRS, coefficient-of-restitution practice for rebound
measurement, and the BO literature on noise handling: SAASBO, qNEHVI,
heteroskedastic/hierarchical noise).

Attached bundle: campaign_summary CSV (= t3-prism-bo-batch-drop-results.csv),
campaign_metrics.json (per-drop rows, 8 specimens), partial_sessions_
metrics.json (the two interrupted-session re-runs), 10 TP4 series-table CSVs
(instrument-independent per-event peaks/durations/delta-v), params.json and
dataset README, our campaign analysis doc and analysis script, the print-
defect study, the PR #97 energy-absorption review, the BO script, its round-2
suggestions CSV, the Sobol design table, and the print key.

Output a single self-contained markdown report we can commit under
edison-trajectories/bo-objectives/. Lead with the conclusions that CHANGE
what we print next.

I’ll first inventory only the numeric files and rig metadata, then compute and write a locked Section A before opening any analysis documents. After that I’ll audit the authors’ reasoning, code, and studies, and produce the commit-ready report.

**Scope lock:** Derived only from the numeric CSV/JSON files and the rig description supplied in the request. I had not read the campaign markdown, print-defect markdown, energy-review markdown, README, analysis scripts, BO script, or suggestion file before writing this block. This text is not to be revised; later changes must be stated as diffs.

## A1. What I would optimize

**Primary formulation:** one objective, **minimize input-adjusted CFC-180 output peak**. With these data I would operationalize that as `t180 = out_180_g / in_180_g`, while retaining `in_180_g` as a nuisance/context variable and imposing an input-severity acceptance window. A preferable future analysis, once enough independent articles exist, is a regression/analysis-of-covariance estimate of output peak at a prespecified input peak (and possibly input pulse shape/delta-v), rather than relying solely on a ratio. The ratio is currently better than raw `out_180_g` for ranking because specimen mean input spans 202.6–231.8 G and output strongly tracks input within specimens (Pearson r = 0.793–0.993). Raw output confounds design with delivered input: for example, amdjwm's low 198.6 G output occurs at the lowest 202.6 G input.

**Candidate classification:**

- **`t180`: valid primary objective, minimize**, conditional on a controlled severity window and mount checks. It directly measures peak attenuation at the specified SAE J211 channel-frequency class. It is dimensionless and normalizes much of the delivered-input variation. A peak ratio can still be biased when numerator and denominator peaks occur at different times or when pulse shape varies, so input peak and delta-v remain diagnostics.
- **`out_180_g`: valid physical endpoint but not a stand-alone objective in this campaign.** It is arguably the payload-facing quantity of greatest engineering interest. Use it as the response in an input-adjusted model or evaluate it at a fixed input severity. With uncontrolled specimen-level input variation, its raw mean is confounded.
- **`in_180_g`: constraint/context, not an objective.** It defines exposure severity. Set an acceptance window or model it as a covariate; optimizing it would optimize the rig/contact rather than protection.
- **`in_dv_ms`: constraint/context and data-quality diagnostic.** It checks impact severity and supports restitution calculations. It is not a specimen performance objective unless the specimen can physically affect the measured base pulse, in which case that feedback itself is a rig-coupling diagnostic.
- **`t1000`: diagnostic and possible safety constraint, not a second coequal objective yet.** It detects high-frequency amplification missed by CFC-180. The cross-specimen rank association with `t180` is high (Spearman rho = 0.929), but broadband values reach 1.230–1.242 for nvxsrv/bag26v. I would cap unacceptable amplification if a payload-relevant threshold is defined rather than optimize it jointly without such a threshold.
- **`t_second_ms`: diagnostic, unusable as a direct protection objective.** It is a timing observation whose event identity must be validated. It does not by itself measure energy.
- **`e_rebound = g t_second/(2 delta_v)`: diagnostic only at present, not an objective.** For ballistic flight, flight time satisfies `t = 2 v_up/g`, hence `g t/(2 delta_v) = v_up/delta_v`: a **velocity ratio**, analogous to a coefficient of restitution only if `delta_v` is the correct incident relative-speed denominator and the detected second event is landing of the same moving body. It is not an energy ratio. A corresponding specific kinetic-energy ratio would be `(g t/(2 delta_v))^2` under restrictive equal-mass/reference assumptions. The label matters physically and for thresholds/noise under squaring, though a strictly monotone square would not change deterministic ordering or the Pareto set for nonnegative values. Event identity is not established by the tabulated metrics, and amdjwm's `t_second_ms` SD is 15.70 ms versus 0.27–1.25 ms for the others, demonstrating detector failure in at least one session.
- **`fn_hz`, `zeta_pct`: opportunistic diagnostics, unusable as campaign-wide objectives.** Missing for three or more specimens/fields and likely conditional on successful mode fitting. They may explain mechanisms but cannot support a common BO response from five specimens.
- **Printed mass:** constraint/covariate, not an objective under the stated constant-solid-CAD-mass goal. Actual mass ranges 18.50–22.04 g, so the intended equality did not hold in printed articles; include measured mass in interpretation and enforce/tighten a tolerance if mass is a design requirement.
- **Derived recommendation:** report an input-adjusted CFC-180 output peak at a fixed reference severity, plus `t180` as a transparent secondary summary. Do not create an energy-absorption objective from peak ratios or hop timing without force/displacement or validated body-velocity measurements.

`t180` and `e_rebound` appear negatively associated, but the evidence does not establish two independent pieces of payload-protection physics. `e_rebound` is nearly identical to `t_second_ms` across specimen means (Pearson r = 0.998) and may reflect one compliance/restitution axis or fixture motion. I therefore would not use a Pareto formulation from these data alone.

## A2. Is multi-objective optimization warranted?

No, not with `t180` and `e_rebound` as currently measured.

Across all eight specimen means, Pearson r(`t180`, `e_rebound`) = **−0.827** (two-sided p = **0.011**), but Spearman rho = **−0.571** (p = **0.139**). Excluding amdjwm because its rebound detection is flagged unreliable gives Pearson r = **−0.844** (p = **0.017**, n = 7) but Spearman rho = **−0.393** (p = **0.383**). This conflict indicates a small-sample, leverage-sensitive relationship rather than a securely ordered trade-off.

The dependence on 6lhxfy is decisive. Among the seven reliable specimens, removing 6lhxfy changes Pearson r to **−0.429** (p = **0.395**, n = 6) and Spearman rho to **−0.029** (p = **0.957**). Removing bag26v instead gives Pearson r = **−0.849** (p = **0.033**) but Spearman rho = **−0.429** (p = **0.397**). Thus the linear anti-correlation is largely anchored by one extreme attenuator/hopper and is not robust in ranks.

For minimizing both values, the measured nondominated set is 6lhxfy, 6nheas, and bpx68c after excluding unreliable amdjwm. That empirical set shows mutual nondominance but does not prove a stable decision-relevant Pareto frontier. With n = 7 reliable articles, one article per geometry, uncertain rebound event identity, and strong single-point leverage, a two-objective BO is unsupported. Optimize CFC-180 attenuation; retain rebound timing/velocity ratio as a diagnostic until independently validated and tied to a payload requirement.

## A3. Noise for each design observation

The experimental unit for design-level optimization is an **independently printed article**, not a drop. The 99 post-warm-up drops are repeated measurements of the same article and cannot reduce print-to-print variability by `sqrt(99)`.

For an article-mean response `y`, use

`Var(y_obs | design) = sigma_print^2 + sigma_session^2 + sigma_drop^2/n_drop`,

with terms defined on a relative/log scale where practical. Given the supplied prior replication scales, my initial fixed noise for `t180` would be a **2% relative standard deviation floor**, combined with the article's drop SEM and, only if the stated 2% print scale excludes remount/session variation, a session term up to 2%:

- if the ~2% print-to-print estimate already comes from independently mounted print tests and therefore includes ordinary session/remount variability: `sigma_t180 = sqrt((0.02*y)^2 + SEM_drop^2)`;
- if print and session components were estimated separately and are independent: `sigma_t180 = sqrt((0.02*y)^2 + sigma_session^2 + SEM_drop^2)`, with `sigma_session` estimated from matched re-mounts rather than automatically taking the maximum observed 2% shift.

At `t180 ~ 1`, the first formula gives SD ~**0.020**, versus the observed per-drop SEM ~0.00017–0.00052. The supplied ~0.0004 treatment is therefore ~50-fold too small in SD and ~2,500-fold too small in variance for predicting a new print.

No print-to-print replication scale is supplied for `e_rebound`, so I would **not invent one and would not hand it to the GP as near-zero fixed noise**. If it were retained after event validation, obtain independent-print replicates and estimate a log-scale article variance. Until then, a transparent provisional sensitivity analysis could use at least a 2% relative floor, `sqrt((0.02*e)^2 + SEM_drop^2)`, but that assumes transfer of the t180 print CV and is not evidentially justified. The correct data-only decision is to keep rebound diagnostic rather than pretend its design-level noise is known.

## A4. Committed answer

1. **Optimize one endpoint:** minimize input-adjusted CFC-180 output peak, using `t180` now and moving toward output-at-fixed-input when replication supports it. Treat input peak/delta-v as exposure controls; constrain gross CFC-1000 amplification; keep rebound and modal fits diagnostic.
2. **Do not run `t180` + `e_rebound` qNEHVI from these eight articles.** The rebound metric is a conditional velocity ratio, not energy; event identity is unvalidated; rank evidence is weak; and the association collapses without 6lhxfy.
3. **Use article-level noise.** For `t180`, start with `sigma = sqrt((0.02*y)^2 + SEM_drop^2)` if the print estimate includes mounting/session effects. Do not use per-drop SEM alone. Do not assign a precise design-level rebound noise without independent-print data.
'''

1→# SOBOL + S0 campaign — first batch analysis (8/9 specimens)
  2→
  3→**Data:** 10 Box uploads posted by @me-madsen on PR #86 (08-21) — 8 specimens
  4→plus 2 partial/interrupted sessions, 942 captures ≈ 8.4 GB, recorded
  5→08-13 → 08-20 under the standing SOP (60 in drop, arrangement B = 1/2 in PU
  6→mat, 150 G trigger on CH5, 100 ms / 1.25 MHz / 2 ms pre-trigger, 101
  7→drops/specimen).
  8→**Script:** [`scripts/analysis/drop_test_campaign_analysis.py`](../scripts/analysis/drop_test_campaign_analysis.py)
  9→(fetch: [`scripts/fetch_box_shared_folder.py`](../scripts/fetch_box_shared_folder.py));
 10→outputs in [`data/drop-tests/sobol-campaign/figures/`](../data/drop-tests/sobol-campaign/figures/)
 11→including the BO ingest file `campaign_summary.csv`.
 12→**Design parameters:** joined from the print key recovered from the issue-#98
 13→`.3mf` (`bo/t3-prism-bo-batch-print-key.csv` on branch
 14→`claude/issue-98-20260821-0103`), committed here as
 15→[`params.json`](../data/drop-tests/sobol-campaign/params.json).
 16→
 17→## 0. TL;DR
 18→
 19→1. **The campaign discriminates.** T = TOP/CH5 (CFC-180) spans
 20→   **0.893 → 1.062 (16.8 %)** across the 8 specimens with within-specimen CV
 21→   0.17–0.48 % — every adjacent pair in the ranking separates at |d| ≥ 2.8.
 22→   **`6lhxfy` (Sobol spec 01) is the first strong attenuator ever measured
 23→   under this SOP (T = 0.893)**, reproduced across two sessions on different
 24→   days to 0.13 %.
 25→2. **A processing fix was required first** (§2): the carriage now arrives
 26→   fast enough that mat contact starts > 2 ms before the 150 G trigger, so
 27→   the 2 ms pre-trigger window rides a +10–20 G contact foot and is no longer
 28→   a valid baseline. Without the fix, Δv reads catastrophically low and — more
 29→   importantly — **T carries a specimen-dependent bias of up to ~5 %**, which
 30→   would have scrambled the BO objective. The fixed pipeline re-baselines on
 31→   the record tail and was validated against the TP4 series tables'
 32→   independent per-event Δv and raw peaks (agreement 1–3 %).
 33→3. **The tower is healthy.** On the corrected (and TP4-corroborated) scale,
 34→   input Δv was 5.03–5.45 m/s all week — at or near the healthy-tower bar —
 35→   and it *improved* through the week (§3). The standing "tower still at
 36→   ~87 % of free-fall" narrative from the 08-10/08-12 sessions was largely
 37→   the same baseline artifact and is corrected below.
 38→4. **For the BO hand-off** (§5): `campaign_summary.csv` has one row per
 39→   specimen with objectives ± sd and design parameters. Two blockers on the
 40→   metadata side: **`amdjwm` (2nd-best specimen, T = 0.980) appears in no
 41→   print key anywhere** — its design parameters are unknown — and the
 42→   `ebdna8` session seen on the TP4 status bar on 08-18 has not been
 43→   uploaded.
 44→
 45→## 1. Sessions
 46→
 47→| specimen | Sobol spec | session (start) | captures | notes |
 48→|---|---|---|--:|---|
 49→| `bag26v` | 08 | 08-13 13:56 | 101/101 | earliest; 5 days before the rest; pre-settings-reset |
 50→| `amdjwm-s1` | **unknown** | 08-17 11:33 | 87/87 | interrupted first attempt |
 51→| `amdjwm` | **unknown** | 08-17 13:57 | 101/101 | full re-run, same day |
 52→| `bpx68c` | S0 (ref) | 08-17 15:19 | 101/101 | = the calibration-check "before" set |
 53→| `autv5r` | 02 | 08-19 15:34 | 103/103 | 2 extra captures (S103/104) after end-of-session pauses — normal drops, kept |
 54→| `6lhxfy-s1` | 01 | 08-19 17:09 | 35/35 | interrupted first attempt |
 55→| `6lhxfy` | 01 | 08-20 13:15 | 101/101 | full re-run next day |
 56→| `9hhbkp` | 00 | 08-20 14:34 | 101/101 | |
 57→| `nvxsrv` | 04 | 08-20 16:13 | 101/101 | one 13 min pause after drop 44 |
 58→| `6nheas` | 05 | 08-20 18:02 | 101/101 | ends 08-21 01:24 UTC |
 59→
 60→942/942 captures are clean real drops — **zero invalid/spurious triggers in
 61→the entire batch**, no channel above 4.7 % of full scale, median cadence
 62→~41–45 s. The 08-13/08-17 sessions predate the 08-18 TP4 settings reset; the
 63→calibration check already verified continuity across it.
 64→
 65→## 2. The pre-trigger contact foot, and why the pipeline needed a fix
 66→
 67→The abc123-era convention baselines every channel on the median of the 2 ms
 68→pre-trigger window. That was valid when it was written. In this batch the
 69→pre-trigger is **not quiet**: CH5 sits +10 to +20 G above the record tail for
 70→the full 2 ms before the trigger (bag26v, the slowest session: +2 G;
 71→08-19/20 sessions: +16 to +20 G). At 5.4 m/s the carriage crosses the mat's
 72→12.7 mm thickness in ~2.3 ms, so early mat compression is already underway
 73→more than 2 ms before the 150 G crossing — the entire pre-trigger window
 74→rides the contact foot.
 75→
 76→Consequences of baselining on the foot:
 77→
 78→- **Δv collapses.** The 15 ms Δv integral picks up the (−foot) offset over
 79→  its whole window: sessions read 2.0–3.5 m/s instead of ~5.3 m/s, and the
 80→  bias *grows within a session* as the mat warms and the foot lengthens —
 81→  manufacturing an apparent "velocity decay" that is not real.
 82→- **T is biased per-specimen.** Peaks are measured relative to the wrong
 83→  zero, and the foot differs between CH5 and the top-vertex channels (they
 84→  see it through different paths), so T shifted by up to ~5 % in a
 85→  specimen-dependent way (e.g. `nvxsrv` 1.074 → 1.024 after the fix,
 86→  `autv5r` 1.077 → 1.041, while `bpx68c` barely moved 1.011 → 1.011).
 87→
 88→**The fix** (committed): `analyze_capture` gains a `baseline="tail"` mode —
 89→each channel is re-zeroed on its median over the final 30 ms of the 100 ms
 90→record — and the campaign pipeline uses it for all sessions. The
 91→default `"pretrigger"` mode is untouched, so every previously committed
 92→analysis reproduces unchanged. Validation against the TP4's own series
 93→tables (computed independently by the DAQ from raw data): per-event CH5 raw
 94→peaks agree to 1–2 %, per-event Δv to 2–3 %, across all 10 sessions. On
 95→clean-pretrigger sessions the two baselines coincide, so the corrected scale
 96→remains comparable to the healthy-tower references.
 97→
 98→**Correction to the standing record.** The same artifact was already
 99→present, smaller, in the 08-10/08-12 rail-maintenance sessions (their TP4
100→series tables read 0.3–0.4 m/s higher than the committed pipeline values,
101→with the gap growing across the week). Two standing conclusions soften:
102→the "settled at 4.55–4.66 m/s ≈ 87 % of free-fall" plateau was an
103→underestimate (TP4 scale: 4.9–5.0 m/s and still rising), and the within-
104→session "mat-rebound decay" in Δv was partly the foot growing rather than
105→physics. Correction notes have been added to the speed-decay and
106→pre/post-grease docs. The qualitative conclusions (greasing produced a real
107→step; no cumulative decay over 100 drops) survive.
108→
109→## 3. Rig health: the tower quietly finished recovering
110→
111→Input Δv (corrected pipeline, corroborated by TP4) by session:
112→
113→| date | session(s) | Δv (m/s) | % of 5.47 free-fall |
114→|---|---|--:|--:|
115→| 08-10 | pre/post-grease | 4.6 (TP4) | 84 % |
116→| 08-11 / 08-12 | speed-decay | 4.9 / 5.0 (TP4) | 90–91 % |
117→| 08-13 | `bag26v` | 5.03 (rising within session) | 92 % |
118→| 08-17 | `amdjwm-s1` / `amdjwm` / `bpx68c` | 5.01 / 5.26 / 5.30 | 92–97 % |
119→| 08-19 | `autv5r` / `6lhxfy-s1` | 5.34 / 5.51 | 98–101 %* |
120→| 08-20 | `6lhxfy` / `9hhbkp` / `nvxsrv` / `6nheas` | 5.37 / 5.45 / 5.33 / 5.26 | 96–100 %* |
121→
122→\* Δv is the full-pulse integral = arrival + rebound speed, so it can
123→slightly exceed the free-fall *arrival* figure; values at ~100 % imply
124→arrival within a few percent of free fall with a small mat rebound.
125→
126→The greasing recovery did not stall at the 08-12 "settled" level — it kept
127→improving with traffic, and by campaign week the tower was effectively at
128→the healthy-tower bar (abc123 healthy reference 5.28–5.35 m/s). Every
129→campaign session lands in a ±4 % Δv band, so impact severity is matched
130→across specimens to about the same tolerance as the input peak (in180
131→203–232 G, partly specimen-mass-dependent).
132→
133→## 4. Campaign results
134→
135→### 4.1 Ranking (stabilized drops, warm-up 2 discarded)
136→
137→| rank | specimen | spec | T180 (CV) | T1000 | e_rebound | t_second | fn / ζ (usable frac) |
138→|--:|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
139→| 1 | `6lhxfy` | 01 | **0.8931 (0.47 %)** | 0.913 | 0.0504 | 55.2 ms | 368 Hz / 10.2 % (0.64) |
140→| 2 | `amdjwm` | ? | **0.9805 (0.26 %)** | 1.007 | 0.030† | 31.8 ms† | 455 Hz / 9.6 % (0.05) |
141→| 3 | `6nheas` | 05 | **0.9970 (0.32 %)** | 0.996 | 0.0402 | 43.2 ms | 322 Hz / 19.3 % (1.00) |
142→| 4 | `bpx68c` | S0 | 1.0111 (0.23 %) | 1.067 | 0.0204 | 22.1 ms | 468 Hz / 16.7 % (0.01) |
143→| 5 | `9hhbkp` | 00 | 1.0183 (0.17 %) | 1.028 | 0.0215 | 23.9 ms | 364 Hz / 11.2 % (0.58) |
144→| 6 | `nvxsrv` | 04 | 1.0275 (0.43 %) | 1.230 | 0.0266 | 28.9 ms | 294 Hz / 31.0 % (0.88) |
145→| 7 | `autv5r` | 02 | 1.0404 (0.34 %) | 1.136 | 0.0268 | 29.2 ms | 386 Hz / 6.4 % (0.39) |
146→| 8 | `bag26v` | 08 | 1.0616 (0.48 %) | 1.242 | 0.0241 | 24.7 ms | — (0.00) |
147→
148→† `amdjwm`'s secondary-event detector is bimodal (CV ~49 %) — its hop lands
149→near a ringdown lobe and the picker alternates between two candidates; its
150→t_second/e_rebound are not reliable this session. All other specimens have
151→e_rebound CV ≤ 4.3 %.
152→
153→ANOVA on T180: F ≈ 2.4 × 10³, p ≈ 0 across 8 specimens; spread 16.8 % with
154→median within-specimen CV 0.33 %. Adjacent-pair gaps and effect sizes
155→(Welch): 6lhxfy→amdjwm 9.8 % (|d| = 25), amdjwm→6nheas 1.7 % (5.7),
156→6nheas→bpx68c 1.4 % (5.0), bpx68c→9hhbkp 0.7 % (3.5), 9hhbkp→nvxsrv 0.9 %
157→(2.8), nvxsrv→autv5r 1.2 % (3.3), autv5r→bag26v 2.0 % (4.8). Figures:
158→[series](../data/drop-tests/sobol-campaign/figures/01_campaign_series.png) ·
159→[ranking](../data/drop-tests/sobol-campaign/figures/02_campaign_ranking.png).
160→
161→**Honest tiering against the known noise floors** (print-to-print ≈ 2 %
162→spread in T; cross-session mount re-seat ≤ ~2 %): the ranking resolves into
163→four design-level tiers — **`6lhxfy` alone** (9.8 % clear of everything),
164→**`amdjwm`/`6nheas`** (attenuating-to-neutral), **the near-unity middle**
165→(`bpx68c`/`9hhbkp`/`nvxsrv`, spanning 1.6 % — *not* mutually resolved at the
166→print level), and **the amplifiers** (`autv5r`, `bag26v`). Within-tier order
167→is statistically real for *these articles* but should not be read as a
168→design difference.
169→
170→### 4.2 The headline: `6lhxfy` (spec 01)
171→
172→T = 0.893 — an 11 % peak reduction relative to the base input, where every
173→previously measured specimen sat within a few % of 1.0 (best ever before:
174→`yqpmx1` ≈ 0.96 at 13 in on the retired hot-glue mount). Its design corner:
175→**thickest struts (9.24 mm), thinnest cables (2.55 mm), highest twist
176→(77.4°), lightest mass (18.50 g)** — the compliant-cable/stiff-strut corner
177→of the Sobol box. It is also the biggest hopper (e_rebound 0.050, hop
178→landing at ~55 ms) and holds T1000 = 0.913, i.e. it attenuates broadband,
179→not just in the CFC-180 band. The BO prior should treat this corner as the
180→live region.
181→
182→### 4.3 Session-to-session repeatability — the free crossover checks
183→
184→The two interrupted sessions are independent re-runs (fresh mount seating,
185→different day for `6lhxfy`):
186→
187→| specimen | session 1 | session 2 | ΔT180 |
188→|---|--:|--:|--:|
189→| `6lhxfy` | 0.8943 (35 drops, 08-19) | 0.8931 (101 drops, 08-20) | **0.13 %** |
190→| `amdjwm` | 0.9862 (87 drops, 08-17 am) | 0.9805 (101 drops, 08-17 pm) | 0.58 % |
191→
192→Both land well inside the ~2 % re-seat envelope — T180 is transferring
193→across sessions far better than the historical worst cases. **T1000 does
194→not transfer** (`amdjwm` 1.159 → 1.007; `6lhxfy` 1.029 → 0.913): the
195→broadband ratio is dominated by mount-coupling HF content, confirming the
196→long-standing choice of CFC-180 T as the primary objective and T1000 as a
197→secondary/diagnostic only. (`autv5r` also drifts +15 % in T1000 *within*
198→its session while T180 stays flat — same lesson.)
199→
200→### 4.4 Drift, ringdown, secondary metrics
201→
202→- **T180 drift within sessions is negligible**: |slope| ≤ 0.016 %/drop
203→  (most ≤ 0.008 %), the two largest with the usual first-drops mat
204→  transient. 101 drops per specimen buys a ±0.05 % standard error on T —
205→  100× tighter than the print-to-print floor; 5–10 recorded drops would
206→  give the same design information (the standing sample-size result).
207→- **e_rebound** spans 0.020–0.050 (2.5×) and correlates with attenuation
208→  (the two best T specimens hop hardest — consistent with energy leaving
209→  through the compliant-cable path rather than transmitting). It remains
210→  the sharpest per-drop discriminator (CV ≤ 2 % for most specimens).
211→- **Ringdown fits** are usable for 5 of 8 specimens (fn 294–468 Hz,
212→  ζ 6–31 %). `bag26v` (0 % usable, the tallest article at H = 105 mm) and
213→  `bpx68c`/`amdjwm` (≤ 5 %) fail the r² gate — their post-impact envelope
214→  is not a single decaying mode. Treat fn/ζ as opportunistic secondary
215→  outputs, not campaign objectives.
216→- **Mat state**: CH5 raw stayed ≤ 4.7 % of full scale everywhere; the PU
217→  mat needed no attention across 942 drops.
218→
219→## 5. BO hand-off
220→
221→[`figures/campaign_summary.csv`](../data/drop-tests/sobol-campaign/figures/campaign_summary.csv)
222→carries one row per specimen: `t180`, `t1000`, `out_180_g`, `in_180_g`,
223→`in_dv_ms`, `t_second_ms`, `e_rebound`, `fn_hz`, `zeta_pct` (mean ± sd
224→each), Δv health verdict, and the design parameters (R, H, twist, strut Ø,
225→cable Ø, mass, spec index) joined from `params.json`. Recommended objective
226→column: `t180_mean` (with `t180_sd`); `e_rebound_mean` as a secondary
227→objective if the BO goes multi-output.
228→
229→**Open items blocking a complete design table:**
230→
231→1. **`amdjwm` maps to no known print.** It is absent from the `.3mf` print
232→   key, the Sobol design table, and every issue/PR in the repo. Its
233→   parameters are blank in the CSV. @me-madsen — which spec is it (a
234→   re-print of 03/06/07? a re-label?), and can its mass be added?
235→2. **`ebdna8` (spec 03)**: the 08-18 TP4 settings screenshot showed the
236→   database sitting on a completed session `ebdna8 - 60 in - 1/2" mat -
237→   101 drops`, but no `ebdna8` upload exists. If that session is real,
238→   uploading it may complete a 9th specimen for free.
239→3. The 9th specimen (tested "tomorrow morning" per the posting comment) and
240→   the slow-motion videos are pending; the pipeline is one command to
241→   re-run when they land.
242→4. Spec 08's official article: the print key flags `dea4ls` (per the .3mf)
243→   vs `bag26v` (per the issue comment) — `bag26v` is what was tested here.
244→
245→## 6. Caveats
246→
247→- **n = 1 article per design** (except the two double-session specimens,
248→  which replicate *sessions*, not prints). The print-defect study put
249→  print-to-print scatter at ~2 % in T — that is the design-resolution
250→  floor for this table, and why the middle tier is unresolved.
251→- `bag26v` ran 5 days before the rest on a slightly slower tower
252→  (Δv 5.03 vs 5.26–5.45); T is severity-robust, but its last-place margin
253→  (2.0 % below `autv5r`) is larger than any plausible session effect.
254→- The Δv health bands in the script were derived on the pre-trigger
255→  baseline; they remain valid on the corrected scale because the two
256→  estimators coincide on clean-pretrigger (healthy-era) data, but
257→  sub-0.1 m/s comparisons across the estimator change should not be made.
258→- `amdjwm`'s t_second/e_rebound are unreliable this session (§4.1 †).
259→- The 2 ms pre-trigger is now structurally too short for a quiet baseline
260→  at healthy-tower speeds. The tail baseline handles it in analysis, but if
261→  the TP4 allows a longer pre-trigger (e.g. 5 ms = 5 %), the foot would be
262→  fully in-record and the estimator debate disappears at the capture level.
263→
264→## 7. Addendum (2026-08-21): why the printed masses vary despite the constant-mass constraint
265→
266→@sgbaird flagged that the measured masses (18.50–22.04 g, CV 5.9 %) vary
267→more than expected given the batch generator's constant-mass constraint
268→(PR #35, `bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py`).
269→
270→**The constraint was implemented and converged.** Route A projects every
271→Sobol design onto the constant-mass manifold by uniform re-scaling, with
272→m\* = 30.95 g defined as the *solid-volume* mass of the S0 reference STLs
273→(ρ_PLA = 1.24, ρ_TPU = 1.21 g/cm³). The committed
274→`bo/t3-prism-bo-batch.csv` shows all 9 designs at 30.90–30.97 g predicted
275→(`mass_ok=True`, tolerance ±0.15 g).
276→
277→**The gap is solid volume vs printed mass.** The slicer prints the PLA
278→struts/joints/housings with walls + sparse infill but the thin TPU cables
279→essentially solid. Regressing the 7 measured masses on the CSV's predicted
280→per-material solid masses (S0's split, 23.42 g PLA + 7.53 g TPU, computed
281→from the committed reference STLs):
282→
283→```
284→measured ≈ 0.565 · m_PLA,solid + 0.986 · m_TPU,solid   (R² = 0.78, resid sd 0.64 g)
285→```
286→
287→PLA prints at ~57 % of solid, TPU at ~99 %. Because the constant-mass
288→projection preserves shape ratios, the PLA/TPU split varies strongly by
289→design (TPU fraction 12–36 %), so each gram of solid mass the design moves
290→from PLA to TPU adds ~0.42 g of printed mass. That deterministically maps
291→the constant-solid-mass batch onto an ~±9 % printed-mass spread — e.g.
292→`6lhxfy` (spec 01, TPU fraction 0.118) is the lightest at 18.50 g while the
293→TPU-rich `9hhbkp`/`6nheas` (0.35–0.36) sit at 21.6–21.7 g. The ±0.3–0.8 g
294→residuals are true print-to-print variance (~3 %), consistent with the
295→print-defect study.
296→
297→**Fix for future batches** (in `bo/t3_prism_sobol_batch.py` on PR #35):
298→either weight the scale solve's per-material volumes by effective print
299→densities (0.565 / 0.986 as fitted — one-line change, but profile-dependent),
300→or iterate the solve on the BambuStudio CLI's sliced per-filament grams,
301→which is exact for the active print profile. Which is "right" depends on
302→what the constraint is for: if the BO comparison is per-gram-of-printed-
303→structure, printed mass is the physical quantity to hold constant.
304→
305→**Side effect worth using:** the fit predicts printed masses for the
306→untested specs — 03 (`ebdna8`) ≈ 20.4 g, 06 ≈ 19.2 g, 07 ≈ 21.5 g. Weighing
307→`amdjwm` (§5 open item 1) against these would help disambiguate which spec
308→it is (a ~19 g reading points at 06, ~21.5 g at 07).
